planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or fall into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade.

directions: This dwarf simplicifolia-type astilbe forms a tidy clump of finely cut, bronze-tinted foliage that holds its color through the season rather than fading to plain green. Loose, arching plumes of soft salmon-pink flowers open in mid to late summer, later than most Arendsii hybrids, extending the astilbe bloom season in a shady border. Keep the soil evenly moist at all times, since simplicifolia types are less drought-tolerant than the chinensis group, and mulch to protect shallow roots through hot Gulf Coast summers. Combine with hostas and ferns at the front of a woodland bed where its smaller stature won't be overwhelmed by larger companions.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit plant profiles

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in partial shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; trim foliage back hard after the spring flush to refresh the clump.

directions: A selection of the native eastern wild geranium found in a Baltimore garden and named for a family member, this cultivar is grown chiefly for its dark chocolate-brown foliage, which holds its color from spring through the growing season. Small lavender-pink, cup-shaped flowers appear above the mounded foliage in late spring and draw in native bees. Shear plants back after the bloom flush fades to keep the foliage compact and to encourage a tidier late-summer mound. Give it morning sun and afternoon shade in warmer climates, since foliage color and vigor both suffer where summers are hottest and driest.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in deep shade in acidic, humus-rich soil that mimics the leaf litter of a hardwood forest floor; keep the crown shallow.

directions: This diminutive evergreen wild ginger from the Piedmont and adjacent Coastal Plain forms slow-spreading clumps of leathery, mottled heart-shaped leaves that stay attractive year-round in deep shade. Small, maroon-red, jug-shaped flowers are produced right at ground level in late winter and spring, usually hidden beneath the leaf litter and pollinated by fungus gnats and other small insects. It is far more compact and slower to spread than the widespread Hexastylis arifolia, making it a good choice for a small woodland rock garden or shaded path edge rather than a large-scale groundcover. Give it undisturbed, consistently moist, well-drained soil and avoid heavy foot traffic near the shallow rhizomes.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated starts only (never wild-collected, as this species is imperiled) in consistently moist, richly organic soil in deep shade near a woodland seep or streambank.

directions: Known only from a handful of counties along spring-fed creek floodplains in central Alabama, this rare evergreen wild ginger produces glossy, mottled heart-shaped leaves and unusually large, showy jug-shaped flowers for the genus, blooming in early spring low against the soil surface. As a globally imperiled (G2) species, it should be sourced only from nurseries that propagate their own stock, never collected from the wild. It wants constantly moist, humus-rich soil and deep shade year-round, closely mimicking the sheltered floodplain habitat where it naturally grows, and resents both drought and standing water. A choice, slow-growing addition to a shaded native plant collection rather than a fast groundcover.
sources: Auburn University Alabama Plant Conservation Alliance

planting.note: Plant divisions in rich, humus-heavy woodland soil in dappled to full shade; allow leaf litter to remain in place as mulch.

directions: Native to rich cove forests of the southern Appalachians, this relative of the more common yellow mandarin bears nodding, bell-shaped, cream flowers speckled with purple in mid-spring, followed by red berries in summer. Its arching stems and broad, veined leaves give it a graceful, layered look reminiscent of Solomon's seal, and it slowly forms a loose colony where happy. Plant in consistently moist, fertile, well-drained woodland soil with a thick leaf-litter mulch to recreate its native cove-forest habitat, and avoid sites that dry out in summer. It combines well with trillium, foamflower, and native ferns in a shaded woodland garden.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Native Plant Trust (New England Wild Flower Society)

planting.note: Plant in cool, moisture-retentive soil in light shade; provide afternoon shade in hot-summer climates to prevent leaf scorch.

directions: This French sport of the classic 'Stairway to Heaven' Jacob's ladder was discovered near Anjou and is prized for its clean cream-and-green variegated, ferny foliage, which brightens a shaded bed even before the violet-blue flower clusters open in late spring. Unlike some variegated sports, its white edging holds well without reverting to solid green or yellowing in strong light, provided it isn't grown in deep shade. It performs best where summers are mild to moderately warm; in hot, humid climates it appreciates constant soil moisture and a cooler microclimate such as the north side of a building or beneath high tree canopy. Deadhead after bloom to tidy the clump and divide every few years as the center thins.

planting.note: Plant along shaded, consistently damp streambanks or seeps in humus-rich soil; this species will not tolerate drying out.

directions: Native to shaded streambanks in the mountains of southern California, this saxifrage relative produces broad, rounded, softly hairy leaves and airy sprays of small white flowers held well above the foliage in late spring to summer. It is naturally found only near running or seeping water and needs soil that never fully dries, making it best suited to a bog garden, streamside planting, or a consistently irrigated shaded bed. Give it full to dappled shade and rich, organic soil, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat. Because it is an uncommon species in cultivation, source plants only from nurseries growing their own stock.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil near a shaded seep, streambank, or wet meadow edge.

directions: This robust western native forms large, sharply lobed and toothed leaves and produces flat-topped clusters of small white, yellow-centered flowers on tall stems through summer. It is naturally found in wet mountain meadows and moist forest understory from California to Montana, so it performs best where soil stays reliably damp and cool, such as beside a shaded pond edge or in a woodland bog garden. Larger and more vigorous than most other Boykinia species, it can anchor the back of a shaded moisture-loving planting alongside rodgersia and ligularia. Avoid hot, dry sites, since foliage will scorch and decline quickly without consistent moisture and shade.
sources: Idaho Fish and Game Species Catalog

planting.note: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in shade to part shade; mulch the crown heavily where winter lows regularly dip below the mid-teens F.

directions: The first commercialized hybrid between Farfugium japonicum and Farfugium hiberniflorum, this patented selection was discovered as a chance seedling in a Georgia garden. It forms a broad clump of glossy, angular-lobed evergreen foliage distinct from the rounder leaves of typical Farfugium japonicum cultivars, and it is valued most for its late display of bright yellow daisy-like flowers held on tall stalks from October into November, well after most other shade perennials have finished blooming. Give it consistently moist, fertile soil and shade from hot afternoon sun, since like other Farfugium it wilts dramatically in dry or overly bright conditions, though it usually recovers with watering. In the Deep South it makes a striking late-season accent for a shaded bed or large container.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil at a woodland edge with filtered morning sun and afternoon shade for best foliage color.

directions: A golden-leaved sport of the popular 'Blackberry Wine' corydalis, this patented cultivar forms a low mound of bright chartreuse-gold, ferny foliage topped from late spring onward by clusters of fragrant, deep purple tubular flowers. The gold color develops best with some filtered morning sun, though the plant tolerates full shade with foliage shifting to a cooler chartreuse-green. Unlike many seed-grown Corydalis, this selection does not self-sow aggressively, making it a tidier choice for a mixed shade border. Keep soil evenly moist and mulched, and expect the plant to go summer-dormant in regions with hot, humid summers, returning reliably the following spring.
